```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.align = "center",
  render = function(x, ...) {
    if (data.table::is.data.table(x) && !data.table::shouldPrint(x)) return(invisible(""))
    if (is.data.frame(x)) x <- knitr::kable(x, digits = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
    knitr::knit_print(x, ...)
  }
)
```

This tutorial runs NICHESv2 on scRNA-seq data with no spatial coordinates: 13,999
human PBMCs, either untreated (`CTRL`) or stimulated with interferon-beta
(`STIM`). You'll score LR signaling between sampled cell pairs and compare the
two conditions.

Without coordinates, nothing tells us which cells really touched. NICHESv2
therefore samples cell pairs within each pair of cell types. Treat the results
as what cell types could signal to each other, not as observed contacts.

With `n.cores = 2`, the slowest step takes about 1 minute and needs about 4 GB of
memory.

## Get the data

The dataset comes from [SeuratData](https://github.com/satijalab/seurat-data),
which isn't on CRAN. Run this once; the download is about 413 MB. SeuratData also
installs the Seurat package, so the first install can take a while.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("remotes", "SeuratObject"))
remotes::install_github("satijalab/seurat-data")
SeuratData::InstallData("ifnb")
```

```{r load}
library(NICHESv2)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(SeuratObject)
library(SeuratData)

data("ifnb")
```

SeuratData objects keep the Seurat version they were saved with.
`extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat()` reads both V4 and V5 objects, so you don't need
to update them first.

## Extract the inputs

```{r extract}
inputs <- extract_NICHESInputs_Seurat(
  seurat.obj = ifnb,
  assay      = "RNA",
  layer      = "counts",
  verbose    = FALSE
)
dim(inputs$count.mtx)

table(inputs$meta.data$stim)
```

Two metadata columns matter here: `stim` holds the condition, and
`seurat_annotations` holds 13 cell types.

## Build the NICHESObject

`sample.col = "stim"` builds edges separately within each condition, so a `CTRL`
cell is never paired with a `STIM` cell. Set it whenever your data has several
samples, donors or conditions. `cell.type.col` is required in this mode, and the
sampling is repeatable through `seed`, which defaults to 42.

```{r create}
obj <- create_NICHESObject(
  count.mtx     = inputs$count.mtx,
  meta.data     = inputs$meta.data,
  LRM.db        = "connectomedb2025",
  species       = "human",
  mode          = "nonspatial",
  sample.col    = "stim",
  cell.type.col = "seurat_annotations",
  method        = "product",
  n.cores       = 2L,
  verbose       = FALSE
)
dim(obj)
```

Every edge stays within one condition:

```{r edges-by-condition}
obj$edge.meta[, .(edges = .N), by = .(Sending.stim, Receiving.stim)]
```

## Compare the conditions

`$edge.meta` carries the condition and cell type of both cells on every edge, so
it joins directly onto the scores. The two conditions have different numbers of
edges, so this divides each total by that number.

```{r compare}
edge.info <- obj$edge.meta[, .(
  edge,
  stim     = Sending.stim,
  sender   = Sending.seurat_annotations,
  receiver = Receiving.seurat_annotations
)]
scores <- merge(obj$edge.data[, .(edge, LRM, score)], edge.info, by = "edge")

n.edges <- edge.info[, .(n.edges = .N), by = stim]

by.condition <- scores[, .(total = sum(score)), by = .(LRM, stim)]
by.condition <- merge(by.condition, n.edges, by = "stim")
by.condition[, mean.per.edge := total / n.edges]

wide <- dcast(by.condition, LRM ~ stim, value.var = "mean.per.edge", fill = 0)
wide[, fold.change := (STIM + 0.01) / (CTRL + 0.01)]
wide[STIM > 0.5][order(-fold.change)][1:5]
```

Interferon-induced chemokines lead this list, which is what we'd expect from this
stimulation. Comparing raw scores between conditions is a simple first look, and
it doesn't correct for differences in sequencing depth.

## Follow one signal

CXCL10 is a classic interferon-induced chemokine, and CXCR3 is its receptor. This
finds the cell-type pairs that carry the strongest `CXCL10|CXCR3` signal after
stimulation.

```{r one-lrm}
cxcl10 <- scores[LRM == "CXCL10|CXCR3" & stim == "STIM"]

pair.edges <- edge.info[stim == "STIM", .(n.edges = .N), by = .(sender, receiver)]
by.pair <- merge(
  cxcl10[, .(total = sum(score)), by = .(sender, receiver)],
  pair.edges,
  by = c("sender", "receiver")
)
by.pair[, mean.per.edge := total / n.edges]

ggplot(by.pair, aes(receiver, sender, fill = mean.per.edge)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Mean score\nper edge", trans = "sqrt") +
  labs(x = "Receiving cell type", y = "Sending cell type",
       title = "CXCL10|CXCR3 after stimulation") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

Dendritic cells and monocytes are the main senders, and CD8 T and NK cells are the
main receivers. Rare cell types such as `Eryth` rest on few edges, so read their
values with care.

## What differs from spatial mode

- `add_neighborhood_composition()` stops in this mode, because neighbor cell types
  would only reflect the sampling.
- `add_neighborhood_edge_agg()` runs, but its neighbors are sampled partners, not
  physical neighbors.
- `export_to_TissuePlex()` needs coordinates, so it applies to spatial data.

## Data source

The data are from Kang HM, Subramaniam M, Targ S, et al. Multiplexed droplet
single-cell RNA-sequencing using natural genetic variation. *Nat Biotechnol*.
2018;36(1):89-94 (GEO: GSE96583). Cell-type labels are from the Satija Lab.
